If you were wonder why is the first Samorost not on Steam, that's because it is a free to play browser game on Amanita Design's official website. The first game was phenomenal for the time it was released at (2003). Blending drawings with photographs of nature and technology creating beautiful graphics. Such art design is unique for this series.

Now with Samorost 2, it still has the unique art style of nature, technology, and cartoons. The game is longer, there are more puzzles, a new story, and better music. Puzzles were difficult at times but can be solved.

If you like point and click games, unique art styles, short games, and/or you played the first Samorost, you should buy this game when it is on sale for a low price.

Edit 05/11/2020
Today an update was released for the 15th anniversary. Glad to see Amanita Design still acknowledges this masterpiece. Better graphics, better interface, remastered sound, and 60 FPS to match up with the other games by Amanita Design, also easy unavoidable achievements.

Samorost 2 is the sequel to its shorter, free predecessor Samorost 1. It is a delightful, stylised point-and-click puzzle game that follows an adorable space gnome after his dog is stolen by aliens.

It is an original and fun experience and a fine example of the somewhat unconventional games of Amanita Design. It can easily be completed in one sitting and has a lot to offer. The stylised, hand-drawn visuals are a stand-out feature of the game and really help to bring to simple but charming narrative to life. The puzzles, despite a few confusing moments, are quite satisfying for the most part, and provide a low level of challenge that helps give the experience a casual feel without becoming dull. I’d definitely recommend this title to fans of point-and-click game but for those who are unsure, the first instalment is free and can be completed in about 15 minutes so is a great way to test the water!

Achievements were super easy to get, just progress through the story for 100% completion and the level select (which was later introduced) made it extremely easy to revisit.

[h1]Short version: 73%[/h1]
Samorost 2 has astonishing art style and fun puzzle/adventure mechanics, but it is too short even for the budget price range.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Amanita Design, in a sense, is a one–trick pony company that makes surreal, textless, and speechless point ‘n’ click puzzle games. Luckily, said trick is a seemingly endless imagination, reflected in each of their products; Samorost 2 (the sequel to their first game which is [url=http://amanita-design.net/samorost-1/]freely available on their web page[/url]) being no exception. 

This incredibly short room-by-room type point ‘n’ click game has an almost childishly simple story: the protagonist’s dog gets kidnapped, and he travels to another asteroid to save his pet. But Samorost 2 isn’t really about the plot; the real content is the creativity. There is more of it present in the alien landscapes (and all the little details they are filled with) than in many large-budget AAA titles. And Samorost 2 manages to present it all under an hour, leading to a really concentrated experience. Sure, it has its price too, but if you like games a little more on the artistic side, then Amanita delivers yet again.

This game changed my life.

Let me start at the beginning. When I was in the third grade, I was constantly bullied by all the other kids in my school. They would call me mean names like 'Titty boy', 'Lugchode', and 'Stinky'. I got so depressed that I decided to just stay in my bed all the time. My mother used to come into my room and beat me with an iron spatula to try and get me to move. I never knew my father...

Six years later and I finally decided it was time for a change. I went back to school and rejoined the third grade, but this time it was worse. I was so much older than all the other kids and no one wanted to be my friend, not even the teacher. One day, during recess, they told me to stand by the school wall and they took turns throwing rocks at me. I suffered severe brain damage and had several broken ribs.

Later that year my mother died. Before she passed away on her death bead, she told me one thing. And I honestly don't remember what it was.

I had to move in with my uncle and I dropped out of school once again. My uncle had an old ratty laptop laying around that he used to let me play solitaire on. I loved the digitized movement of the cards so much that I decided to steal my uncles money from his safe and buy a real gaming computer.

Fast forward ten years and I was officially a master at every video game I touched. Then I discovered this little indie title called "Samorost 2". From that moment on everything changed. My mother and father came back to life, all the third graders in my old class came forward and apologized to me. Even my teacher!

I now live happily in a mansion with my seven wives, twelve super-cars, and billions of dollars.

Thank you "Samorost 2", I will be forever grateful to you.

I love the way Amanita Design makes their games - a lot of love clearly went into the worldbuilding. You're a little man in his PJs exploring floating mushrooms that have been uprooted from the ground and left in space! Your spaceship is made out of a discarded can of weenies! There's a sewage tank and the water stains look like a pastoral farmscape! So many little beautiful details that are worth the price of admission alone.

I'm not so much a fan of the puzzle-solving. Most of the puzzles are fine and are nice little breaks from the art, but sometimes they are a bit of a pain when trying to decipher context clues in a small Flash window. (FYI, this game was released ten years ago and it holds up well, though it's hard to see things sometimes.) [quote]“The real voyage of discovery consists not in seeking new landscapes, but in having new eyes.” 
― Marcel Proust[/quote]

In one word, [i]Samorost 2[/i] is a “voyage”.

[h1]Foreword[/h1]
I highly recommend trying out the original [i]Samorost[/i] before purchasing this installment. Available for free on the Amanita Design website, it's a fine point of reference to experience Amanita's style, and whether or not you'll appreciate it.

[h1]The premise[/h1]
[i]Samorost 2[/i] is an excellent -- albeit short -- sequel to the first installment of the series. The conflict starts when your cute dog gets stolen by creatures of vile intent, and you set after them to retrieve your loyal boy. From then on, you'll encounter obstacles and puzzles in the form of, among other things, bug-eating creatures, flying seals (?) and even wild dandelions.

[h1]Where it excels[/h1]
As it is the trademark of every Amanita Design game, when it comes to sound and visual effects [i]Samorost 2[/i] leaves nothing to be desired, and paired with intuitive puzzles and a delightful story, it is able to tell its tale in a smooth ride that allows its players to drink in its gorgeous scenery and poignant character design.

[h1]Where it falls short[/h1]
Sadly, [i]Samorost 2[/i] feels just a little bit too short. The game can be completed in roughly 1 hour, making one wish for more, despite the rounded conclusion.

To add to that, sometimes it is difficult to tell which elements are interactive, so some become harder not due to their design, but due to the fact that oftentimes their elements need to be, first and foremost, visually hunted down. This is an issue that Amanita has most certainly overcome in their latest titles, but which [i]Samorost 2[/i] falls prey to one too many times.

Lastly, the very last puzzle [spoiler](taxi puzzle)[/spoiler]  can be infuriating, as it requires a bit of timing that can lead to some redoing. So head's up.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
I highly recommend [i]Samorost 2[/i] if you're already fond of any other Amanita Design game. However, if you've never been introduced to the studio before – aside from [i]Samorost 1[/i] – titles like [i]Botanicula[/i] and [i]Machinarium[/i] may prove for a smoother first ride.

Last but not least, don't forget to keep [i]Samorost 3[/i] in mind after playing this one, as it is certainly one of Amanita's best titles, and a worthy and memorable conclusion to this involving tale.

As he won't abandon his friend in need, he bravely follows the aliens to their home planet! On his journey, he needs to be rather resourceful and use every wit to get both of them safely home.

Puzzles are pretty straightforward although some can be a little bit obscure to realize (also the final puzzle with seals can be sadly somewhat tedious). There is no penalty if you do something wrongly, so if you don't know what to do next just try clicking on everything on the screen!

All in all it's a very pleasant game and I can only recommend it. :3

[h1] A THINKING-TINKERING KIND OF GAME [/h1]

I love mechanical-type puzzles, the ones where you have to adjust valves and tinker with gears, water levels, or electrical components to solve them.  Samorost 2 fit the bill with lots of mechanical-type puzzles to solve, in fact, everything about this adventure was a quest requiring a little bit of tinkering and a lot of "outside the box" thinking! But then again, I've never been abducted by Aliens...allegedly.

This is a thinking-tinkering adventure quest,  heck, it's more like an Escape the [strike] Room [/strike] er, Planet game! 

Sanorost embarks on an intergalactic quest in the middle of the night to retrieve his retriever from pup-poaching Aliens. He boards his not-quite-so-trusty Rocket Ship and travels to a not-so-distant planet, where he quickly discovers that he needs help figuring out the lay of the land, so to speak,...(AKA the person behind the mouse controller; you, the player, and undoubtedly the mastermind of "Operation Where's Betty White When You Need Her?"

Each level Samorost progresses to is a  puzzle that needs to be solved by tinkering with various sections of the scene. At first glance, there doesn't seem to be anything solvable because this game is different than typical Adventure games where you scour the scene searching for a useful object to help you progress.  In this game, I found it helpful to just sit back for a moment and watch how "things that go bump in the alien night"  interact within the scene or with each other. After watching the scene, you will probably notice a pattern or skill set that something has.

The tasks are solved logically but in an Alien way. The developer did an amazing job of creatively "thinking outside the box"  and using elements within the scene itself. I can honestly say that I didn't need a walkthrough to solve this game and was still able to complete the game in 1.2 hours! I enjoyed every minute of the game and didn't feel frustrated at any point...that's what I call great entertainment!

"Samorost 2" is a point-and-click game that tells a surreal story of a space gnome whose dog just got kidnapped by mischievous aliens. You will help the gnome to find its dog by solving different kind of puzzles. This game has an interesting plot, enhanced graphics with full-screen support, beautiful art, humouros sound effects, engaging puzzles and 13 achievements.
It's a short game as it took me only 20 minutes to finish it and get all the achievements (all the achievements can be acquired in one sitting). It has only one ending and there is a save feature, so you can restart or continue the game from a selected chapter. I would give it a 2/10 difficulty rating as the gameplay is minimal and the instructions are pretty clear during the whole game (you need to solve the puzzles and finish the story).
After playing "Samorost 1", which is a free-to-play game on Steam (you can find it here - https://store.steampowered.com/app/1580970/Samorost_1/), I decided to try more games from this developer. 
"Samorost 2", released in 2009, is the second game from the trilogy (you can find the third game on Steam as well) and it  has been developed by Amanita Design (Jakub Dvorsky's indie game studio), same company responsible for other well-known titles such as "Machinarium" or "CHUCHEL". In this game you will need to guide a space gnome on a quest across a couple of bizarre asteroids in order to rescue your dog from some aliens who kidnapped him. As you explore the asteroids and meet their strange inhabitants, you'll have to solve a few puzzles in order to progress. 
I didn't encounter any issues while playing the game and I was very much impressed by the beautiful visuals. The game's backgrounds often combine organic with inorganic elements and each scene in the game contains movement. The music (composed by Tomáš Dvořák) was extremely relaxing and created a wonderful atmosphere to just sit back and relax while solving the puzzles. The puzzles were not too difficult, although difficult enough that it presented a bit of a challenge. The story was really cute and well represented without the use of any word dialogue (there is only a little voice-acting in form of non-legible utterances).
As a recommendation for developer, I would like to suggest adding a hint button which may improve the experience for a lot of players. I would also like to mention that I got this game on a sale (for 99 eurocents) and I think that its initial price (of 4.99 euros) is a little too high for 20 minutes of gameplay.  
All things considered, I will definitely try more games from this developer and I would recommend this game to players that like surreal games or to the casual players that are trying new games/doing playthroughs.

Amanita Design are masters of establishing exotic audio-visual aesthetics. The team pushed the visual quality given that this is a 2005 flash game and Tomas Dvorak's (aka Floex) soundtrack is incredibly immersive and unique. That said, I give this game a recommendation with some caveats. 

While the overall design is great, the low resolution square screen space makes the point-and-click aspect of the game challenging when the click space for an interactive component on the screen is only a few pixels wide. I was able to complete the game without a guide, but felt that certain moments of progress were attributed to pure luck. There are a few moments where an object has to be toggle picked up and then used on another object in the screen space. There is a good chance your patience will wear thin at these parts, as the click area has to be so specific that a general pass of the area might not be enough to trigger the next part of the puzzle sequence. Finally, there was a timed puzzle that was janky given the strange interactivity of objects in a Flash game. The game can  be completed in 30 minutes, but might take you longer as it did for me. 

Gameplay issues aside, is this game worth experiencing? Yes, but I would say this game is oriented more to those interested in exploring a foreign world than for point-and-click purists. The artistry was what stuck with me more than the game mechanics.

[h1]
A Short Click and Play Game
[/h1]
Samorost was originally released in 2003 and it is still available on Amanita Design's website. This is the only game in the series that is available as a free game. I really love games by Amanita, with Machinarium currently being by favorite. They're quirky, they're cute, and they're fun to figure out. I highly recommend Samorost 2 if you're already fond of any other Amanita Design game. However, if you've never been introduced to the studio before (aside from Samorost 1) titles like Botanicula and Machinarium may prove for a smoother first ride. Samorost 2 isn’t really about the plot; the real content is the creativity. There is more of it present in the alien landscapes and all the little details they are filled with than in many large-budget AAA titles. And Samorost 2 manages to present it all under an hour, leading to a really concentrated experience. Sure, it has its price too, but if you like games a little more on the artistic side, then Amanita delivers yet again.

Although very short, Samorost is a great point-and-click adventure game which has a very unique artwork. The gameplay is very simple - we look for clickable objects on every screen and try to solve the puzzles that represent obstacles before Gnome could proceed any further to reach his goal. I really like the game's surrealistic world with its unique creatures - above all, Gnome itself, who lives on an asteroid full of plants.

[h1]
Story
[/h1]
We control a cute space gnome. In this game, we are trying to find our dog by going after those who came to our planet and kidnapped our dog. As we explore the planet they went to, we meet the people there and then we solve some puzzles to move forward. From then on, you'll encounter obstacles and puzzles in the form of, among other things, bug-eating creatures, flying seals and even wild dandelions. It doesn't take long to finish but it's a lovely little adventure and I think it's well worth experiencing.

Playing Samorost 2 for the first time shortly after its release was a magical experience. As a young player, I was immediately drawn to its charming, otherworldly visuals and its unique, quirky style. Now, revisiting it as an adult, I can appreciate even more how beautifully crafted and innovative this game truly is.

One of the standout features of Samorost 2 is its stunning graphics. Even by today's standards, the game's art style remains captivating and timeless. The meticulous detail in the environments, combined with the whimsical and surreal design, creates a visual experience that is both enchanting and memorable. Every scene feels like a piece of art, inviting players to explore its intricacies.

The game's uniqueness extends beyond its visuals. The story, while simple, is engaging and presented in a way that draws you into the protagonist's adventure. The quirky characters and imaginative settings make for an unforgettable journey that stands out in the point-and-click adventure genre.

As a young player, I remember feeling like Samorost 2 was an incredibly long and complex game. It's funny to think back on how my perception has changed; the game is relatively short and straightforward compared to modern titles. However, this brevity does not detract from its charm. Instead, it adds to the nostalgic value, reminding me of a time when every puzzle and interaction felt like a grand adventure.

Unlike most games of its kind, there’s no text, no dialogue, and no character conveniently telling you what they need or where you should go next. Instead, the game relies entirely on your curiosity and intuition. Progress comes from noticing how elements in the environment connect, often in a way that feels obvious in hindsight, yet delightfully puzzling in the moment.

That’s the magic of Samorost 2, its puzzles are simple, almost self-evident, but they require you to observe, poke around, and piece together tiny cause-and-effect chains. It’s a bit like solving a whimsical, minimalist Rube Goldberg machine without being told what the final motion should look like. The game is never truly difficult, if you have a little patience, you’ll naturally work your way from one scene to the next. Some puzzles click instantly and make you feel clever; others might have you scratching your head for a few minutes. But you’ll get there, and watching the little white-onesie protagonist continue his journey is always satisfying.

The art style is one of the game’s biggest strengths. It blends photo-bashed, surreal landscapes with simple, flat-shaded characters in a way that’s strangely harmonious. The contrast gives each scene a dreamy, handcrafted feel. The audio design supports this vibe beautifully, calm, unobtrusive, and atmospheric, it nudges the experience forward without ever drawing attention away from the visuals or puzzles.

I rarely play point-and-click adventure games, but I must concede that this one is making me re-consider the credibility of the medium as a  whole. As you can see from the screenshots, the game's visuals are comprised mostly of backgrounds created from stitched-together phoographic elements with meticulously hand-drawn aimated elements in the foreground. The game is not wholly 2-Dimensional, however, as certain interactions will cause the characters to move further away or closer. This art style in combination with the varied and highly atmospheric ambient music gives the game an excellent "feel" when played for the first time, and the clarinet in particular is put to good use in portraying the mood of the characters.

The puzzles are challenging but not impossible, and most require you to think "outside the box," with a few involving the need for careful timing or requiring you to complete steps in a certain order which, although often unclear to begin with, will have real consequences, causing you to have to repeat an often difficult section if you fail to execute the steps in order or in time. The solutions are often amusing, and the cut-scenes that follow equally so. However, I must admit to consulting the walkthrough occasionally. Mostly this was due to my own inability to see a solution, but sometimes it was because it is not clear what can be interacted with and what cannot. 

This leads me to my one real complaint: The fact that it is not always clear what can be interacted with and what cannot results in same "pixel-searching" on the part of the player, whereby one clicks systematically on every object visible on the screen before proceeding to click on every five-millimetre-square section of screen-space boustrophedonically starting in the top-left corner, regardless of whether or not it contains an object or not.

What surprises me the most is that both this game and it's prequel managed to be so art-like, atmospheric and high in quality, despite being made so long ago and utilising only the capabilities of Adobe Flash Player.

To summarise:

+Unique appearance 
+Excellent soundscape
+Amusing solutions to some puzzles
+As much as it pains me to say so, the characters and story can be described accurately as "cute"
+Happy ending
+Price (I bought the Amanita package on sale, but even even at $5.00 for 2-3hrs per play it's still better value than a rollercoaster or a movie. And it can be re-used.)

Samarost 2 is a cute, charming game. After playing the extremely short Samarost 1 on the Amanita website, I wanted to play this one. Though this one was on the short side too, I enjoyed walking around the weird alien world and doing the quirky puzzles. The puzzles were pretty easy though and barely required any thought.

My only gripe with this game is that the cursor doesn’t have a glow, or any sort of mouseover indicator to let you know that a particular item is clickable. Combine this with a low-resolution window on a larger screen and you can barely see the clickable items. This leaves you pixel hunting throughout the screen for objects that are clickable. Adding to this, some items become clickable when something occurs and conversely, some become unclickable when another thing occurs. So, more than the puzzles themselves, I found myself wrestling with the UI to know what was clickable and what was not. There was an entire area towards the end I couldn’t get to because I didn’t find the clickable pixel.

Nevertheless, these issues, though frustrating, didn’t cause me too much hassle for me to dislike the game. It’s just that my 2-hour playthrough could’ve easily been a lot shorter without the frustrating pixel hunts.

I’ll still give it a good rating and would recommend it to anyone looking for a short, quirky adventure.

Final verdict: 7/10.

Samorost2 is a point-and-click adventure puzzle game from Amanita Design.  Amanita’s quirky characters, worlds, and stories are truly unique, even in the indie game landscape.  In Samorost2, follow a cute space gnome as he searches for his alien-abducted dog.

Samorost1 is available for free, right on Amanita’s website!  Play that first, and if you like it, invest in Samorost2.  Samorost1 is a Flash-based game, and Samorost2 expands on its ideas and you can really see that the developer learned from the first game and it outpaces the first both technically and gameplay-wise.  In each game, you will guide the little gnome from static screen to screen, clicking objects in the environment and figuring out how to open the path forward.

The gameplay here is simple.  If something looks interesting, click on it.  It will either help you progress, make a cool sound effect, or do nothing at all!  Most of the game you will be squinting at the screen to try and find the one object that turns your cursor into a hand (indicating a clickable object), or trying to determine the correct order to click things in.  Often it is not 100% apparent exactly what you’re supposed to do, but the options are generally limited enough that you can stumble across the solution pretty easily.  This is not an adventure game that makes you feel very clever for having figured it out, but rather one where the atmosphere and the weird surroundings make you curious and inquisitive to see how things fit together.  Real-world knowledge of how things work is not very useful here, where items behave in unexpected ways.  The joy in this game is not figuring it out based on what you already know, but by being inquisitive.

The graphics are one of the outstanding things about this game.  Simple, but evocative.  You’ll see an old oil can used as a spaceship.  You’ll see mossy tree trunks used as massive structures filled with life.  Strange alien landscapes made out of things we see everyday bring a refreshing look to a genre that is often all about either retro pixelation or brown realism.  Also, Samorost2 can be run on almost any old Windows machine, due to its incredibly simple Flash programming.

The audio in Samorost1/2 is really interesting.  Ambient, often soft and eerie, you’ll be displaced by the music and thrust into this odd world.  The sound effects are also incredibly detailed.  Animals will make unique sounds, alien machines will clank and whir strangely, and wind will blow through the “trees”, lending a beautiful atmosphere to the game.

Obtuse puzzle games like this can be frustrating at times, where you see a bunch of clickable objects, but have no idea how to put them together.  Even when you do manage to blindly stumble into the solution, that is often unsatisfying.  However, Samorost drips with such charm and quirky joy that you’ll often find you do not care.  The uniqueness of the alien landscapes, coupled with the cuteness of the gnome and his dog (and the smoking bro), will likely make you enjoy yourself regardless.

Samorost1 and 2 are interesting games for more than just their own sake.  Amanita Design went on to make some of the most highly-praised adventure games of the past few years, including Machinarium and Botanicula.  Some of the features that made those games so great are present here, in Samorost, in their infancy.  Amanita’s first foray into adventure games is well worth your time, if only to see where it all began.

Samorost 2, developed by Amanita Design, is a charming and surreal point-and-click adventure that continues the studio’s tradition of crafting visually stunning, quietly humorous, and deeply imaginative games. As the sequel to the original Samorost, this second installment expands upon the ideas introduced in its predecessor while maintaining the minimalist design, whimsical storytelling, and organic world-building that define the series. Originally released in 2005 and later re-released on Steam with enhancements, Samorost 2 is a relatively short but beautifully crafted experience that draws players into a strange and captivating universe.

The game begins with a peaceful moment: the protagonist, a small white-clad space gnome, tends to his home planet alongside his dog. Their tranquil life is quickly disrupted when alien visitors abduct the dog, prompting the gnome to embark on a rescue mission that spans multiple small planets. What follows is a series of increasingly bizarre and clever scenarios in which the gnome must solve puzzles, interact with strange inhabitants, and navigate surreal environments. Like its predecessor, Samorost 2 features no spoken dialogue or written text, instead relying entirely on visual storytelling, intuitive cues, and expressive animations to guide the player through the narrative.

The gameplay in Samorost 2 is rooted in classic point-and-click mechanics, but it is notable for how seamlessly it integrates logic, whimsy, and experimentation. Puzzles are environmental in nature and often involve observing how elements in the world react to each other. Solutions require a combination of patience, curiosity, and a willingness to explore possibilities. Some interactions are deliberately obscure, but never to the point of frustration. Instead, the game’s structure encourages players to playfully engage with the environment, rewarding attentiveness and creative thinking rather than punishing missteps.

What makes Samorost 2 truly special is its aesthetic. The visual design blends hand-drawn illustrations with manipulated photographic textures to create lush, alien worlds that feel organic, lived-in, and slightly uncanny. Every scene is packed with detail, from wriggling alien flora to strange machines and tiny insect-like creatures going about their routines. The environments are whimsical yet eerie, evoking a sense of wonder and curiosity that is rarely matched in the genre. It’s a world that feels like a lucid dream—one where the rules are just familiar enough to be recognizable, but strange enough to feel magical.

Complementing the visuals is an equally enchanting soundtrack by Czech composer Tomáš Dvořák, also known as Floex. The music is sparse but memorable, alternating between playful melodies and ambient soundscapes that match the mood of each scene. Sound design plays a subtle but essential role in puzzle-solving, and the whimsical effects—clicks, squeaks, chirps, and hums—give personality to the game’s many curious denizens. The absence of voice acting is never felt as a loss; instead, it enhances the sense of immersion, allowing players to interpret emotions and story beats through animation and sound alone.

Despite its many strengths, Samorost 2 is not a long game. Most players will complete it in under an hour, though a few puzzles may slow progress depending on individual intuition. The game is split into two chapters, with the second chapter introducing new challenges and environments, but the narrative arc remains simple and contained. Some players might find its brevity a drawback, especially by modern standards, but others will appreciate its tight pacing and focused design. There’s no filler here—just pure, distilled creative vision.

The re-released version on Steam includes updated visuals, a remastered soundtrack, and a few quality-of-life improvements, such as better resolution support and streamlined interface tweaks. These enhancements bring the game more in line with modern expectations while preserving the original charm and integrity of the experience. For fans of Amanita Design’s later titles, like Machinarium or Samorost 3, this version of Samorost 2 serves as both a nostalgic look back and a delightful standalone adventure in its own right.

In conclusion, Samorost 2 is a small but beautifully realized game that showcases Amanita Design’s unique voice in the world of indie games. It’s a celebration of imagination, artistic expression, and non-verbal storytelling—a gentle, surreal journey that evokes curiosity and wonder at every turn. Though short in length, it leaves a lasting impression through its memorable world, clever puzzles, and hauntingly lovely soundtrack. For anyone seeking a quiet, contemplative, and visually striking escape, Samorost 2 remains a timeless and essential experience on Steam.

Samorost 2 builds upon the quaint charm of its predecessor, expanding Amanita Design’s surreal universe while retaining the whimsical essence that made the original so endearing. The game invites players to once again guide the tiny gnome protagonist across mysterious planets, solving puzzles that feel both organic and imaginative, all within a compact, self-contained adventure.

In terms of storytelling, Samorost 2 continues the tradition of silent narrative. Without dialogue or text, the game conveys its tale through visual cues, animations and interactions. The journey remains delightfully abstract, but it’s emotionally resonant: small gestures, subtle humor and inventive world-building give the adventure personality and charm.

The gameplay is deceptively simple but cleverly designed. Point-and-click mechanics remain intuitive, yet puzzles have grown more intricate, often requiring multiple steps or lateral thinking. Each challenge is seamlessly integrated with the environment, encouraging players to explore every corner and experiment with interactive elements. The satisfaction comes from discovery, as solutions feel earned rather than handed to the player.

Aesthetically, Samorost 2 elevates the visual style of the first game. The combination of hand drawn art and photomontage is richer, with more layers and finer detail. The environments are alive with quirky, interactive objects, curious creatures and a palpable sense of place that invites lingering exploration. Complementing this is a playful and occasionally haunting soundtrack, perfectly attuned to the game’s dreamlike atmosphere.

Overall, Samorost 2 refines the formula of the original while adding depth and polish. It’s a brief but memorable experience that emphasizes creativity, curiosity and exploration. For those who value artistry and imagination in gaming, this title remains a shining example of how minimalism can deliver maximum impact.

[b]A cult classic adventure game you must try before Samorost 3[/b]

Samorost 2 is a sequel to the original free-to-play Samorost, an online Flash cult classic game created by Jakub Dvorsky long time ago. This sequel has been developed by Amanita Design (Jakub Dvorsky's indie game studio), same company responsible for other well-known titles such as Machinarium or CHUCHEL. Samorost 2 is a great point-and-click adventure game where once again, you play as the same small gnome character from the first game, on a quest to save your stolen dog. Along the way you’ll encounter some very bizarre and stranger creatures. 

Short and simple, this is a game you can complete in a single afternoon. As in the previous game, the player moves from one enchanting level to another after solving inventive puzzles or overcoming obstacles. Most puzzles are just pixel hunts, because essentially all you need to do is hit the few hotspots in the right order. Sadly, the lack of a proper hint system makes some ilolligical parts quite hard but in the other hand some of them are pretty obvious as well.

The world you explore is so enchanting, with the same art direction as the original with touches of Asian influence. The game's backgrounds often combine organic with inorganic elements and  each scene in the game contains movement, and the creatures, gadgets, plants and insects are beautifully animated. There is hardly any text or dialog in the game and little voice-acting in form of non-legible utterances. The music was composed by Tomáš Dvořák, and like what he did for the previous game, the soundtracks in Samorost 2 are pleasant to listen to.

All in all, this game as a single piece isn't so bad but neither so great. However, Samorost is a worthy series that fully deserves your support. You would like to play this one and the original game title before to really go for Samorost 3, a real masterpiece from the new era.

Ok so here is my review for Samorost 2.

[b] Art [/b] Like the other Samorost games Samorost 2 has some amazing art. It is a little more hand drawn looking than 3 whether this is a pro or a con is up to you but I personally enjoy it and it has a nice feel all around. The art is very consistent and really flows from one place to another. Everything has a nice mix of the look of a picture, an abstract world and random items in the everyday world. The only gripe I have about the art is the lack of screen shots. I really wish you could take screen shots in this game and I would really like it if they added that (don’t expect them to because of the platform its running on and the fact that it’s an older game). Although it is really a con I would still totally recommend the game.

[b] Story [/b] The story in this game like in the others is very simple and nice. I doesn’t make you think too hard and there are really no decisions to make. This might not be for some people but it makes the game wonderful to play when you just wana check out and enjoy some free time. There are 2 main objectives of the story or game and each brings you some fun times and is decorated with amazing art and sound not to mention some great puzzles. The game took me around 4 hours to complete with some help and really feels like a treat instead of a grind. 

[b] Sound [/b] The sound is really an excellent feature of this game. It incorporates great and odd voicing and smooth music/sounds. The environment is constantly being noisy and involves and draws you in with interesting and fun sound cues. I highly recommend playing this game with a headset and if you don’t I don’t think you will get the true feel of the game. 

[b] Puzzles [/b] The puzzles are very nice and unlike samorost 3 and have a clear answer based on the environment or plot of the story. This makes the experience much more enjoyable and you will not need a guide to finish the game if you really wana do it by your own wits and cunning :P. I used a guide that I will link in the description. Most of the puzzles are not too easy and not too hard and can take from 5 to 10 minutes depending on the use of a guide. If a guide is used then you can quickly 2 to 3 minutes. I used a guide on most of the harder puzzles and it took me roughly 4 hours to complete.

[b] Feel [/b] You can tell that this is an older and homemade game. It’s not to polished and is a little bit clunky at times. This is where Samorost 3 and Samorost 2 really differ. You can’t free roam as much in this game. This make the world just a little less inviting but doesn’t really effect the gameplay in a negative way. Sometimes you will get stuck in a puzzle and will have to complete it before you can move or back track again. This is somewhat of a double-edged sword and made it easier to complete the game in a quick run. The other edge is that it also makes it less of a joy to free roam in and just enjoying the environment. In all I would prefer the ability to free roam and be able to walk in various places instead of a semi small area. The last thing is that sometimes your lil gnome or whatever he is will not look natural going or exiting a building and seems to get caught on the walls or doors. Although this games mechanics are not as good as its successors it’s still usually very clean and has a noice feel to it. 

[b] Characters [/b] The characters really gave this game its fantastical feel. There are a variety of distinct species and subsets of characters to interact with. Most of them have a purpose and they really give the game its amazing fun and different feel.

[b] Final Takeaway [/b] This is a great game and a must have if you enjoy fun little games with amazing art and a good old calming feel. The puzzles are great for a relaxing time and generate just enough difficulty to make them feel interesting. The music and sounds are crisp and real and it doesn’t feel like any other game (besides the other Amanita Design games). It’s a steal for $5 USD and you can find it for $2.50 USD or under on sale most of the time. I would highly recommend this game before buying Samorost 3 because if you like this then you will also like 3. Below are a few links to videos and guides I found usefully in the game.

The puzzles are mostly sensible. However, they're also fairly simple and solving them doesn't provide much satisfaction. To be fair, it's difficult to balance those two.
Most puzzles are confined to a single scene. A few require traveling between two or three screens.
There are few solution steps that don't make logical sense. However, those can usually be figured out given the limited number of options.

I did look up an answer for one of the puzzles. This was for a few reasons:
- I didn't expect there was a timing element.
- The step required me to direct Gnome to do something. Gnome sometimes does actions automatically, and I didn't expect to have to direct Gnome in this case. 
- Gnome's action wasn't a satisfactory solution. 


Some of the puzzles require actions that I dislike:
- Actions revolving around mild toilet humor (farts, urine, vomit). At least for me, it wasn't funny. Maybe young kids would like it.
- Killing bugs. They are just bugs, but it's not as if the bugs are bad guys or threatening Gnome. In some cases, it also doesn't make much logical sense about why you need to kill them.
- Poisoning someone
   -- Again, who you poison isn't even necessarily a bad guy. There's also no information provided about what to expect when you give the person the poison. It could be killing them for all you know. I didn't understand why we were poisoning the person and the game doesn't justify it. There were simpler, less harmful, and less risky alternatives available to Gnome.
- Repeating the same action more than once. Once I "get" the puzzle, I don't want to have to waste time on repetition.

[h3]Graphics[/h3]
The graphics are a mix of the following contrasting elements:
- realistic (yet also surreal) backgrounds
- simply designed animated characters that are colored flat and borderless

The 15th anniversary update in 2020 increased the resolution of the graphics with AI-based upscaling. However, the backgrounds still appear somewhat low resolution and pixelated.

That said, still props to the devs for doing the update. It also added Mac support and full screen mode.

[h3]Music/Sound[/h3]

Samorost 2, originally released in 2005 and remastered in 2020, is a short point-and-click adventure with absurd art, quirky humor, and a surreal alien world. While it has nostalgic charm and appeals to a niche audience, its gameplay might not hold up for everyone.

Pros:

Unique art style: The absurd, alien-inspired visuals stand out, though some textures in the remaster are inconsistent in resolution.

Achievement-friendly: Completing all achievements is straightforward—all you need to do is finish the game.

Affordable and short: It’s a cheap game that you can finish in under an hour.

Runs well on Steam Deck: The touchscreen-like controls make pointing and clicking intuitive and enhance the experience.

Helpful Steam community guide: Steam’s  guide section is incredibly useful, helping you avoid getting stuck and making the game more enjoyable.

Cons:

Puzzles lack clarity: The game doesn’t teach its mechanics well, like needing multiple clicks to interact with some objects, which might leave new players stuck.

No clear objectives: Upon entering a stage, the game doesn’t always provide a clear goal. You only realize the objective after solving the puzzle, which makes figuring out the logic more challenging. While this might be a hallmark of older point-and-click games, it doesn’t make the experience more enjoyable.

Alien logic: The puzzles can feel unintuitive due to the surreal setting, often requiring trial-and-error.

Progression bug:

[spoiler] After completing a puzzle, there’s a button on a recliner that may not work unless you restart the game. If you encounter this issue, simply reload the game, and the button should be functional. [/spoiler]

Overall:
Samorost 2 is best suited for fans of absurd art and humor or seasoned point-and-click players familiar with the genre’s quirks. For newcomers or those seeking a polished experience, it may feel more frustrating than enjoyable. While it offers nostalgic charm and a quick, inexpensive playthrough, its lack of modern quality-of-life features might not resonate with everyone.

This is a "neutral" recommendation. The game is pretty and has good parts, but it also has some unfortunate design flaws.

This game looks pretty, looks casual, and it is mostly fine. However, it has a few issues that will prevent casual players from making progress without a guide. I don't consider myself a casual player, but I also had to use a guide a few too many times.

- It's not clear what's interactive and what's not. So you either have to move the mouse around to see the pointer change, or keep clicking everywhere.
- If you're playing on a touch screen (e.g. Steam Deck), you don't benefit from the mouse pointer changes. Thus, you'll be probably tapping everywhere.
- While most of the interaction is done by plain clicking, a few objects require click-and-drag. That can be very surprising and leave players stuck for a while.
- While most of the game is forgiving, there are four or five time-based puzzles that require precision while clicking. It's also not obvious these are time-based. Even less obvious due to the surreal nature of this world.
- The last puzzle is time-based involving three clicks, and failing it requires re-playing a long (one or two minutes) section.

These are explicit gameplay design decisions. They could be changed to be more forgiving or more obvious, and the game would still be an enjoyable experience. Unfortunately, these issues make the game less enjoyable and even a chore. When I faced those issues, I lost my immersion to the game world and started fighting the game controls and the game mechanics. I'd rather stay immersed in the world and the story, instead.

Samorost 2 is short. It's going to resonate differently with each individual. I personally found nothing particularly fantastic about it. The original Samorost sets itself apart by using close-up photographs of various objects, mostly forestial, to create the illusion of large landscapes. Samorost 2 relies more on a traditional hand-drawn approach, and struggles to be as visually interesting as the first game, which is available for free on the Amanita Design website.

Samorost 2's music, as usual for an Amanita game, is top-notch, and one of its highlights.

There are only a handful of puzzles in the game, and the design is problematic in certain areas. For example, the point-and-click interface allows you to click anywhere on the screen to interact with any object - yet for certain objects, it requires your little hero character to be standing in a certain area, making it easy to dismiss something as non-interactive when in fact you were just incorrectly positioned.

And the very last puzzle of the game is a frustrating chore - it's a timing-based puzzle, already something I don't care for, and if you get it wrong, which is highly likely as it takes a bit of trial-and-error to figure out, you have to grind out the game's previous puzzle to get back into the situation needed to try your luck again. The previous puzzle involves collecting animal farts. Of the 90 minutes I played the game, I spent maybe 30 minutes collecting animal farts. That kind of pisses me off.

So I can't really recommend the game. It's not exciting, challenging, or visually appealing enough to merit even a short playthrough, and spending money on it seems silly. It should have been a free flash release. Skip this and play the excellent Machinarium.
